When I was ten, an old amplifier. More specifically, I had bought a broken amplifier, replaced the fuse and had on the dining room table with the cover off. A small capacitor exploded sending fluffy paper all over the place.

I learned about what happens when bridge rectifiers fall that day. Got many good years out of that amplifier even though only one channel worked.

Several years ago I built a modest, but decent sounding stereo for my vehicle that included a sub and amp. One day the sub stopped working, and after tinkering with things I decided that it had to be the amp that failed.

The speaker looked fine, it was new, and hitting the wires going directly into it with a jolt caused it to respond, that's when I decided that I would take the amp apart and try to repair the issue. The amp looked alright but I didn't have anything else to test it on, not without a lot of hassle.

I couldn't find anything visibly wrong with it so I started testing components, which, due to a lack of focus on my part, led to damage that couldn't be easily or cheaply repaired--lesson learned. In the end, I bought a new amp just to find out that it still didn't work. What the hell? Right.

That's when I turned my attention to the speaker. After close inspection I discovered that the plastic protrusion that was part of the terminals contained a fuse, which had blown...the documentation overlooked this fact. Plus, it was the only sub that I had ever come across to contain such a fuse.

I was out a bit of money over the situation, but I learned to go over everything thoroughly before taking drastic steps. Oops!

Oops :)

For future reference, tapping a AA battery onto the terminals will give a small pop sound to confirm your speaker is OK.
